record.title: EvoPathBench tests whether self-evolving agents retain and adapt capabilities
record.summary: A September 21 preprint introduces EvoPathBench, an author-built benchmark for tracking persistent agent memory and skill updates across 1,800 ordered task streams. It tests held-out generalization, retention after unrelated learning and adaptation after a rule changes. In the reported experiments, gains often weakened under distribution shift, retention loss was concentrated in some paths, and no method showed reliable rule adaptation; adaptation effects were not statistically significant after Holm correction. The paper also reports that update-selection safeguards reduce harmful accepted changes but miss more beneficial ones. These results come from fixed configurations in constructed trading environments combining public Binance data and calibrated synthetic trajectories. They are not independently reproduced and do not establish deployed-agent or real-market performance.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce EvoPathBench, a benchmark of 1,800 ordered streams across six task families and two market layers. It evaluates persistent memory/skill artifact updates using held-out checkpoint tests for learning generalization, capability retention and rule adaptation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the reported experiments, gains on familiar conditions often weakened under distribution shift, retention losses were concentrated in a subset of paths, and no evaluated method showed reliable rule adaptation. No revision effect remained statistically significant after Holm correction.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that candidate selection is a major bottleneck: safeguards reduced accepted harmful updates but also lowered capture and recall and increased missed improvements. The benchmark reports selected artifact-level methods on its own constructed market tasks.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The preprint does not establish that its measured effects generalize to deployed agents, other model or tool configurations, or real trading outcomes; the research desk did not independently reproduce the results.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent execution or reproduction of the benchmark results was performed.
The benchmark uses public Binance Spot data combined with calibrated synthetic trajectories; evidence does not establish validity in other agent deployments or actual trading.
Rule-adaptation rankings are not reliable evidence of method superiority because no revision effect remains statistically significant after Holm correction.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported benchmark results hold, checkpoint-level measurement across transfer, retention and rule reversal could expose failures hidden by endpoint-only scores and help evaluate persistent agent updates. Consequences are meaningful for evaluation design, but the evidence is a single author-run benchmark on constructed trading tasks; it does not establish deployed-agent or real-market effects. The score reflects potential consequence, not confidence.
limitations: All empirical findings are reported in one preprint; the research desk did not execute code or independently reproduce them.
The benchmark comprises constructed task streams combining public Binance Spot data with calibrated synthetic trajectories, not actual trading outcomes.
Results cover ten configurations with fixed base models, tools and executors and five update opportunities; transfer beyond these configurations is unknown.
The paper reports no rule-revision effect statistically significant after Holm correction; point-estimate rankings should not be read as reliable superiority.
The benchmark and method comparisons are author-designed; independent assessment of task validity, API/model variability and release reproducibility remains open.

It tests held-out generalization, retention after unrelated learning and adaptation after a rule changes. In the reported experiments, gains often weakened under distribution shift, retention loss was concentrated in some paths, and no method showed reliable rule adaptation; adaptation effects were not statistically significant after Holm correction. The paper also reports that update-selection safeguards reduce harmful accepted changes but miss more beneficial ones. These results come from fixed configurations in constructed trading environments combining public Binance data and calibrated synthetic trajectories. technical.claimed_result: Across ten configurations, reported near-distribution capability gains often weakened or reversed under transfer; retention losses were uneven across trajectories; no rule-adaptation effect remained significant after Holm correction. Candidate selection safeguards reduced harmful updates while reducing gain capture and increasing missed improvements.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper describes a benchmark with 1,800 streams across three stream templates, six task families and two market layers. Six frozen artifact checkpoints are evaluated on held-out episodes. These are author-reported design and evaluation details, not independently reproduced by the research desk.
technical.mechanism: EvoPathBench fixes the base model, tools and executor while allowing explicit persistent artifacts such as memories, skills or workflow rules to change. Accumulation, interference and reversal streams probe transfer, retention and adaptation; matched held-out evaluations compare evolving methods with a non-evolving baseline and with artifacts disabled.
technical.regime: The authors compare ten configurations over five update opportunities and six artifact checkpoints. The environment combines public Binance Spot price data with calibrated synthetic trajectories; it includes exogenous and endogenous market layers. Findings concern artifact-level self-evolution under these constructed tasks.
technical.strongest_baseline: The non-evolving Baseline is used for capability evolution and retention comparisons; disabling artifact access provides a state-use comparison. The paper also compares memory and skill-evolution methods.

brief.title: EvoPathBench tests whether self-evolving agents retain and adapt capabilities
brief.why_it_matters: Persistent memories and skills can change an agent over a sequence of tasks, while a final score can hide what it learned, lost or failed to revise. EvoPathBench reports a structured way to test transfer, retention and adaptation at frozen checkpoints. Its results point to weaknesses in transfer and update selection, but the evidence is an author-run benchmark using constructed trading tasks; the paper does not show real-world trading or deployed-agent effects.
